title: US Approves $5.75B Saudi JDAM and Tank-Engine Package as Japan Seeks Record $55.6B AI-Centric Budget
subhead: Washington cleared a large precision-munitions sale to Riyadh while Tokyo pushed a record defense budget centered on AI-driven command and mass-produced 3D-printed interceptor drones. Russia, meanwhile, readied its biggest African airshow display since the war.

sections.heading: US Clears $5.75B Saudi Package: JDAM-ER Bombs and Abrams Engines
sections.body:
On September 4, the U.S. State Department approved a possible $5.0 billion Foreign Military Sale to Saudi Arabia covering 10,004 JDAM-ER guidance kits and matching bomb bodies, along with a concurrent $750 million sale for 60 AGT-1500 tank engines, according to Army Recognition reporting on the Defense Security Cooperation Agency notifications. The munitions are split almost evenly by unit count — 5,004 KMU-572 kits with 500-lb BLU-111 bombs and 5,000 KMU-556 kits with 2,000-lb BLU-117 bombs — but nearly 80 percent of total bomb mass sits in the heavier penetration class, giving Riyadh a deep magazine of hardened-target ordnance alongside cheaper lighter weapons.

JDAM-ER wing kits extend a baseline unguided bomb's reach to more than 74 kilometers, adding standoff precision-strike capability. The tank engines keep the M1 Abrams fleet mobile. The combined $5.75 billion covers spares, fuzes, target detectors, repair support and engineering services.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a volume rather than capability statement: two years into the Gulf conflict, Washington is replenishing a Gulf partner's precision-strike and mobility stocks at scale, signaling durable US munitions production capacity and a strategic commitment to Saudi standoff power.

sections.heading: Japan Seeks Record $55.6B Budget With AI at the Center
sections.body:
Japan's Ministry of Defense submitted a record 8.9-trillion-yen ($55.6 billion) defense budget request for fiscal 2027, with artificial intelligence, unmanned systems and long-range weapons as the core themes, the Defense Post and Associated Press report. A centerpiece is an integrated AI command-and-control platform meant to accelerate battlefield assessments and target selection, including an 'AI orchestrator' concept that would coordinate multiple AI systems and combine US-developed technologies with Japan's own models.

Two supporting procurements reinforce the same direction. ATLA has signed a mass-production agreement for Terra Drone's Terra B1 interceptor, a 3D-printed, rocket-powered drone built to shoot down one-way attack drones like Iran's Shahed and anti-radar loitering munitions such as the IAI Harpy — a decision processed in roughly three months, far faster than the usual one-to-two-year defense timeline, per SSBCrack News. Separately, Japan's Defense Ministry contracted NTT Data to build a satellite that fuses sensor data for military targeting, with human-authorization details undisclosed.
sections.whyItMatters: Tokyo's buildup is shifting from hardware quantities to software and speed: AI-driven decision cycles, distributed 3D-printed production to survive supply-chain attacks, and space-based targeting all point to a force designed to fight a fast, drone-heavy war rather than a traditional attrition campaign.

sections.heading: Russia Readies Largest African Airshow Push in Years
sections.body:
Russia will land at the El Alamein International Airshow (September 8-10) with one of its most extensive air-weaponry displays in recent years, Aviacionline reports, with Rosoboronexport coordinating and several systems presented for the first time. The centerpiece is the Su-57E, flown with a weapons package including RVV-MD2 and RVV-BD air-to-air missiles and Kh-38MLE, Kh-69 and anti-radiation Kh-58UShKE air-to-surface weapons. Moscow is also showcasing the S-71M and S-71K unmanned systems designed to be launched from fifth-generation fighters — a Russian take on manned-unmanned teaming.

The lineup spans drones, loitering munitions, air defense and counter-drone systems, all presented as combat-proven. Moscow is using Egypt as a platform to regain prominence in African and Middle Eastern markets as the Ukraine war strains its production base but also provides battlefield validation for export pitches.
sections.whyItMatters: This is Russia's most direct bid to reclaim defense-export share in the Global South since the war began, betting that battlefield-tested unmanned and counter-drone systems — not just the flagship fighter — are what African and Middle Eastern buyers actually want now.

sections.heading: HII Secures First Funding for Fifth Ford-Class Carrier
sections.body: On September 4, the U.S. Navy awarded Huntington Ingalls Industries a $336.112 million cost-only undefinitized contract action to buy long-lead material for the future USS William J. Clinton (CVN-82), Army Recognition reports. The funding, drawn from FY2026 Shipbuilding and Conversion appropriations, secures reactor equipment, heavy forgings and propulsion hardware at Newport News Shipbuilding ahead of a planned 2027 keel laying, with launch around 2032 and commissioning by 2036. The action shifts the fifth Gerald R. Ford-class carrier from fiscal planning into active industrial procurement under a $22.3 billion carrier-replacement program budget through FY2031.
sections.whyItMatters: The award locks in the multi-year, single-supplier rhythm of US carrier construction and confirms the Ford-class line stays funded through a second carrier named for a living former president — a concrete industrial commitment amid broader Pentagon leadership churn.

sections.heading: Croatia Taps Hanwha for Chunmoo as K9 Gains Drone Fire Control
sections.body:
Croatia is finalizing a €435.2 million contract with South Korea's Hanwha Aerospace for 18 K239 Chunmoo multiple-launch rocket systems, expected to be signed September 8, Army Recognition reports, with payments spread from 2026 to 2029 and 85 percent of the package delivered during 2028. The Chunmoo — which carries up to twice as many ready-to-fire rockets per launcher as HIMARS — replaces legacy M92 Vulkan and BM-21 Grad launchers and adds two range brackets (160 km and 290 km) not in Croatia's existing HIMARS ammunition. The procurement integrates Poland's WB Group TOPAZ command-and-control system and lifts Croatia's planned long-range rocket-launcher fleet to 26 vehicles.

On a parallel track, Hanwha unveiled a K9 operating concept at the fifth K9 User Club in Tartu, Estonia, integrating a VTOL fire-guidance drone directly into the self-propelled howitzer's fire direction system. The concept aims to compress the call-for-fire sequence from 15-20 minutes to under 60 seconds by using a single continuous-custody UAV for detection, coordinate calculation, impact observation and battle-damage assessment.
sections.whyItMatters: South Korea is consolidating its position as the artillery and rocket artillery supplier of choice in Europe — competing directly with US HIMARS and European alternatives — while deepening the drone-into-sensor-shooter integration that is becoming the defining feature of modern fire support.

sections.heading: Lockheed Scales CH-53K Output as Contractors Push Production Up
sections.body:
Lockheed Martin Chief Financial Officer Evan Scott said the company could double CH-53K heavy-lift helicopter deliveries in 2026 from last year's level and potentially double again in 2027, describing the ramp as part of a broader output increase across Sikorsky, Defence Industry EU reports. All four Sikorsky platforms are expected to deliver more aircraft this year than in 2025, while F-16, C-130 and ten munitions programs within Missiles and Fire Control are also increasing deliveries. Lockheed raised its full-year Rotary and Mission Systems sales outlook to $17.7-$18.1 billion with profit of $1.86-$1.89 billion. 'We are in a scaling mode right now,' Scott said.

In a smaller but adjacent signal, satcom maker Kymeta announced a $20 million DoD order on September 4 for flat-panel satellite terminals, integrated mobility packages and software-defined multi-orbit connectivity to support tactical communications, per SatNews.
sections.whyItMatters: The top US contractor is converting wartime demand and prior backlog into actual delivery volume increases, an early test of whether the defense industrial base can translate higher budgets into faster fielding without hitting supplier bottlenecks.

bottomLine: Two themes dominated a busy week in defense procurement: Washington and Tokyo both moved to buy war-fighting capacity at scale — a $5.75 billion Saudi precision-munitions package and a record $55.6 billion Japanese budget built around AI-driven command and mass-producible interceptor drones — while Russia pressed its own export counteroffensive in Africa and South Korea kept winning European artillery orders. The through-line is production and speed: every major actor is trying to shorten the gap between decision, contract and delivery, in a market where ammunition depth, drone defense and software-defined targeting now matter as much as platform specs.
sources: Army Recognition, Defense Post, Associated Press, SSBCrack News, Aviacionline, SatNews, Defence Industry EU, Euro-SD
